description:
Which source names describe where a flow is rather than what the substance is.

A substance gathers several source flows, and the ones whose names lost the contest for the substance's published name are carried as alternative names so that an inventory written against a source list still finds the substance (#113). Most of those names are worth keeping -- `Dichloroethylene`, `Quizalofop-P-tefuryl`, ecoinvent's `Ethane, 1,1,2-trichloro-1,2,2-trifluoro-, CFC-113` -- and a large minority are not, because they name a flow and not a substance.

`Hafnium, In Ground` is the case. Hafnium in the ground and hafnium anywhere else are the same substance; `In Ground` says which flow, and the list already says that on the flow's context. Publishing it as another name for hafnium would tell a reader that the substance is called that, which it is not. `Occupation, Annual Crop, Irrigated` is the same thing from the other end: the whole name describes a land use, and the substance it resolves to is a land class.

So this file is the vocabulary that separates the two, and it is data rather than a pattern in code because every entry is a curator's reading of what a vendor meant by a word. Measured on the 2026-08-18 build merging ecoinvent 3.12 and 3.8, it rejects 392 of the 598 candidate names.

There is a third test and it is not here, because it is not a membership question: a comma-separated segment containing a per-cent sign states a concentration -- `Aluminium, 24% In Bauxite, 11% In Crude Ore, In Ground`, `Pt, Pt 2.5E-4%, Pd 7.3E-4%, ... In Ore, In Ground` -- and a concentration is an ore grade, which is a property of the deposit and not a name of the metal. That rule is stated in `flow_layers/synonyms.py` where it is applied.

land_flow_prefixes.comment: A name whose first comma-separated segment is one of these describes a land use over a period, which is what the flow measures; the substance behind it is a land class. ecoinvent names every one of its land flows this way, 182 of the 392 rejections. Matched on the whole first segment rather than as a prefix of the string, so a substance whose name merely begins with these letters is untouched.

places.comment: A comma-separated segment reading `in <one of these>` says where the substance was found or measured, not what it is. Every value here was read off the names this rejects: `in ground` accounts for 200 of them, `in ore` and `in mixed ore` for 17 each, and the rest are single figures. `natural gas` is here because `Methane, In Natural Gas` is methane in a deposit and not a name for methane; the substance natural gas is a different row with its own registry number.

chemical_classes.comment: Names that name a family of chemicals rather than any one member. A source list that uses one as a flow name is naming a substance it could have named properly -- EF 3.1's `polyhaloalkene` is HFO-1234yf, CAS 754-12-1, and ships under both spellings -- and once the flow is renamed for the member, the class word must not come back as a synonym: a synonym asserts `this substance is also called X`, and a family name is a name for every member at once, so it is a name for none of them. Same reasoning as a place: the word says what kind of thing the substance is, not what it is called. (#116)
